title: Compare Social Position, Duties and Freedom
content:
Chapter 1 showed different kinds of work. Social status means a person's position in society. It is more than a job: it can affect recognized rights, duties and freedom. The same task does not mean two people have the same choices.

Use a specific example rather than one pyramid for every island. Juan de Plasencia, a Spanish missionary writing in 1589, described Tagalog communities using terms including maharlika and different forms of alipin. His account is one outside view, written after Spanish arrival, not the voice of every community.

In that account, maharlika were free people with duties to a datu. Aliping namamahay could live in their own homes and have property while owing service. Aliping sa gigilid served within another household, with greater restrictions; the account says people in this category could be sold. These were unequal conditions, not simply voluntary jobs.

Other sources use terms such as timawa, and social arrangements varied. Do not automatically match every Tagalog label with a Visayan label. Compare the place, source, duties and freedoms before deciding whether two groups were alike.
clues: These cards summarize one 1589 account of Tagalog communities. The descriptions must not be applied unchanged to every region or time.
The account distinguishes free people with service duties from different forms of dependent service. Owing work did not give everyone the same freedom.
CulturEd also describes timawa as free people with obligations. A similar description is a reason to investigate, not proof that every regional group had identical rights.
task: Two accounts use different names for social groups. What should you compare before calling the groups identical?
Their place, time, rights and duties
Only whether their names sound similar
Only the clothes in a teaching picture
Only the order of names on a poster
reason: A social name alone is not enough. Compare the source, place and described rights and duties, while recognizing differences in freedom.
definition: A recognized place in a society that can affect rights, duties and choices.

glossary.definition: Something a person is expected or required to do.
A responsibility or required service; it was not always freely chosen.
An account or item that gives information about the past.
A person's position in society; it can affect recognized rights, duties and choices.

title: Your Turn: Compare Two People
content:
Now apply the comparison to two made-up people. Their names and circumstances are teaching examples, not biographies of actual historical individuals.

Person A owes an agreed task at a gathering, but can choose to visit relatives after finishing. Person B must continue required service in another household and cannot decide freely to leave. Both are working, yet the information describes different limits on choice. We cannot assign their exact historical titles from these brief descriptions alone.

Work through the evidence. Step 1. Identify what each person must do. Step 2. Identify which choices each can make. Step 3. Explain the difference without judging the worth of either person. A duty is something someone is expected or required to do. Freedom of choice concerns what they can decide for themselves.

Not every duty was freely accepted, and describing a custom does not make an unequal arrangement fair. Do not turn historical social labels into names for classmates or a game of owning people. Use the supplied cases to understand experiences and their limits.
clues: The fictional case says A can choose to visit relatives after the task. It does not say A has no duties at all.
The fictional case says B cannot freely choose to leave required household service. That is a restriction on choice, not evidence of lower personal worth.
The cases do not provide enough regional and historical detail to assign exact group names. Explain the stated difference instead of inventing a title.
task: What conclusion is supported by the two fictional cases?
Both people have duties, but the cases describe unequal freedom to choose
Having any duty means both have identical rights
A restriction on Person B means B has less worth as a person
A brief work description identifies every exact historical status
reason: The cases describe different choices and restrictions. Social inequality concerns conditions and power, not differences in human worth.
definition: Differences in recognized rights, opportunities or freedom within a society.

glossary.definition: A limit on what a person can choose or do.
The value of a person, which is not determined by historical social position.

title: Field Journal: Connect Community Experiences
content:
Connect the mission discoveries. A datu could help guide community affairs. Family ties could connect relatives across households. Customs could be passed through stories, advice and everyday practice. Social positions could affect rights and duties, so people did not experience community life in one identical way.

Use the comparison method in your journal: name the source and setting, describe a responsibility, identify a choice or restriction, then state what remains uncertain. The title of a leader alone does not explain every action, and seeing people cooperate does not prove that everyone had equal freedom.

Our Tagalog source example is not a description of all Philippine communities. The fictional cases help you practise comparing choices; they do not give an exact title to every person. Save useful opened clues if you want to revisit the evidence. Next, the beliefs-and-traditions mission asks how people understood their world and passed on knowledge, while keeping differences among communities visible.
clues: A leader, a family relationship and a local custom can affect the same situation. Ask how each contributes rather than choosing one explanation for everything.
Two people can both work while having different control over their time. Cooperation is not proof of equal rights or freedom.
A strong comparison identifies its setting and uncertainty. It avoids treating one colonial account or one fictional case as the story of every community.
task: Which report best connects the mission evidence?
Leadership, relatives, customs and social position could shape different experiences within a community
Everyone who worked together necessarily had equal freedom
One historical title explains every person in every region
A fictional case gives the full history of all Philippine society
reason: The report connects several influences on community life while recognizing different experiences and limits to the sources.
definition: Examining similarities and differences using stated evidence.

glossary.definition: A practice learned and passed on within a community.
